{noformat}select provider_id, provider_name,
count(distinct case when order_state = 'failed' then order_id else null end) / count(distinct order_id) as rate_failed,
count(distinct case when order_state = 'failed' and supply_refunds_eur > 0 then order_id else null end) / count(distinct case when order_state = 'failed' then order_id else null end) as rate_paid_failed,
count(distinct case when order_state = 'failed' then order_id else null end) as count_failed_orders,
count(distinct case when order_state = 'failed' and supply_refunds_eur > 0 then order_id else null end) as count_paid_failed_orders,
count(distinct case when order_state = 'delivered' then order_id else null end) as count_delivered_orders,
sum(order_gmv_eur) as gmv, 
sum(supply_refunds_eur) as refund
from ng_delivery_spark.fact_order_delivery
where order_created_date >= date_add(current_date, -14)
group by 1,2 
having count(distinct case when order_state = 'failed' and supply_refunds_eur > 0 then order_id else null end) > 2
and count(distinct case when order_state = 'failed' then order_id else null end) / count(distinct order_id) > 0.3
order by 3 desc{noformat}

Hey,

What we knew previously of Blast Dispatch was that if driver A grabs the order and driver B loses it, their AR/DS will not be affected. However, there are some corner cases here, and in general some driver-facing notes that we previously didn’t know to account for, and therefore these were not added to the KB’s. 



* Drivers may ‘lose’ an order offer to another driver and they will see a note saying ‘*Order has been accepted by another driver’*.
** It is okay to let the driver know that we may offer the same order to multiple drivers to ensure that the rider doesn’t have to wait long to be matched with a driver.
* If the driver wants to know how many drivers we blast the offer to:
** Can be anywhere from 1-5, depending on marketplace conditions and drivers' availability. In simple words, it varies, but between 1-5 is the default.
* *Losing an order to another driver does not decrease the acceptance rate or driver score values* (as also mentioned in the updated article 🚗 [Driver: I have a question about my Acceptance Rate|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360007473734?country=global&language=en]) HOWEVER, if an order is dispatched and none of the drivers accept it, the AR decreases for all parties. 

In admin, under acceptance rate details: 
*- If neither driver responds*, both are marked as *"Driver did not respond"*. -> AR decrease 
*- If D1 accepts*, D2 is marked as *"Offer was Rejected"* instead of "Did Not Respond." -> D2 AR does not decrease 
*- If D1 rejects and D2 does not respond*, then: 
-- D1 is marked as *"Driver Rejected" ->* AR decreases for D1 
-- D2 is marked as *"Do Not Respond" ->* AR decreases for D2



Can we clarify this logic in the AR article? 🙂 



Also, I am [double-checking the auto-acceptance logic|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C06JZ101TL2/p1746534400220779], as it may be that they changed that compared to the 1st iteration.

*CS Announcement Draft*

Hi, everyone! 👋🏻

*WHAT*
Instead of offering orders to drivers one-by-one until one of them accepts, we may blast the same order to multiple drivers simultaneously, to reduce the time we spend looking for a driver.
In v2, we use the average ETA of the 5 nearest drivers as a proxy for determining how many drivers to blast to (previously, it was a static number of drivers configured on a city level).

*WHERE/WHEN*
*06.05-03.06  (4 weeks)*
* BE: Antwerpen, Brussels
* CH: Zurich
* FR: Paris, Angers, Bordeaux, Caen, Dijon, Grenoble, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes, Nimes - Avignon, Orléans, Reims, Rennes, Rouen, Saint-Etienne, Strasbourg, Toulon, Tours, Marseille
* GB: Bristol, Edinburgh, London
* IE: Dublin
* NL: Amsterdam
* PL: Lodz, Poznan, Silesia, Trojmiasto
* PT: Porto
* SE: Gothenburg, Malmö

*HOW*
Guidelines, which should cover the main concerns we anticipate:
* Drivers may ‘lose’ an order offer to another driver, and they will see a note saying ‘*Order has been accepted by another driver’*.
- It is okay to let the driver know that we may offer the same order to multiple drivers to ensure that the rider doesn’t have to wait long to be matched with a driver.
* If the driver wants to know how many drivers we blast the offer to:
- Can be anywhere from 1-5, depending on marketplace conditions and drivers' availability. In simple words, it varies, but between 1-5 is the default.
* Auto-acceptance logic:
- TBA
* *Losing an order to another driver does not decrease the acceptance rate or driver score values,* as also mentioned in the article 🚗 [Driver: I have a question about my Acceptance Rate|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/360007473734?country=global&language=en]. However, if an order is dispatched and none of the drivers accept it, the AR does decrease for all parties. 

An example with 2 drivers:
*- If neither driver responds*, both are marked as *"Driver did not respond"*. -> AR decreases for both
*- If D1 accepts*, D2 is marked as *"Offer was Rejected"* instead of "Did Not Respond." -> D2 AR does not decrease
*- If D1 rejects and D2 does not respond*, then:
-- D1 is marked as *"Driver Rejected" ->* AR decreases for D1
-- D2 is marked as *"Do Not Respond" ->* AR decreases for D2

In case of any issues or questions, please share the information with your TL.

Thank you and have a nice day! 🌸

*List of technical and organisation measures suggested by ShareForce*

*Annex 5 – Technical and Organisational Measures*
# *Security Overview*
## The Processor uses Heroku, one of the world's leading Platform as a Service (“*PaaS*”) providers, to run the Processor’s application. Heroku in turn uses Amazon Web Services (“*AWS*”), the world's largest cloud computing provider, for its infrastructure requirements. 
## The Processor has selected that its servers are specifically based in the European Union Region (Ireland), where strict data protection policies are in place. 
## The Processor's solution is fully hosted in Ireland, where it uses Amazon web services. The following services are used in this region: (i) web servers, (ii) database, (iii) background workers, and (iv) task queues. The Processor’s database backups are located in the Frankfurt region of AWS.
## AWS servers comply with the European Union protection directive. AWS servers have already obtained approval from the European Union data protection authorities, known as the Article 29 Working Party, of the AWS Data Processing Addendum and Model Clauses to enable the transfer of data outside Europe, including to the United States of America. 
## The AWS Data Processing Addendum is available to all AWS customers that are processing personal data whether they are established in Europe or a global company operating in the European Economic Area (available at [https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/data-privacy-faq/|https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/data-privacy-faq/|smart-link] ). 
# *User Security*
## Users of the System are required to select strong passwords which are encrypted before being stored in the database and uses industry-best-practice hashing algorithms. 
## In addition, all Users have the option to enable two-factor authentication for their own account. The Controller can also select to enforce the two-factor authentication for all its Users.
# *Processor Security*
## All data in transit is encrypted using a secure sockets layer (SSL) or hypertext transfer protocol secure (HTTPS), including all data between the User's browser and the server, to protect sensitive data transmitted to and from the application. 
## Only two people at the Processor have access to the servers.
## Access to the servers is protected using double authentication mechanisms. To prevent unauthorised account access, the Processor uses a strong passphrase for its Heroku user account and stores secure shell (SSH) keys securely to prevent disclosure.
## The following protection mechanisms are in place by the Processor:
### cross-site scripting (XSS) protection;
### cross-site request forgery (CSRF) protection;
### security query language (SQL) injection protection;
### click-jacking protection;
### use of secure cookies;
### secure password storage - passwords are never stored in plain text; and
### platform as a service (PaaS) security standards.
## Heroku applies security controls at every layer, from physical to application, isolating customer applications and data.
## Heroku’s physical infrastructure is hosted and managed within AWS secure data centres, and it utilises AWS technology. AWS continually manages risk and undergoes recurring assessments to ensure compliance with industry standards. Amazon’s data centre operations have been accredited under:
### ISO 27001;
### SOC 1 and SOC 2/SSAE 16/ISAE 3402 (previously SAS 70 Type II);
### PCI Level 1;
### FISMA Moderate; and
### Sarbanes-Oxley (SOX).
## Heroku utilises ISO 27001 and FISMA-certified data centres managed by AWS. AWS has many years of experience in designing, constructing, and operating large-scale data centres. This experience has been applied to the AWS platform and infrastructure. AWS data centres are housed in nondescript facilities, and critical facilities have extensive setbacks and military-grade perimeter control beams, as well as other natural boundary protection. Physical access is strictly controlled both at the perimeter and at building ingress points by professional security staff utilising video surveillance, state-of-the-art intrusion detection systems, and other electronic means. Authorised staff must pass two-factor authentication no fewer than three times to access data centre floors. All visitors and contractors are required to present identification, sign in, and continually be escorted by authorised staff.
# *Firewalls*
## Firewalls are utilised to restrict access to systems from external networks and between systems internally. 
## By default, all access is denied and only explicitly allowed ports and protocols are allowed based on business need. Each system is assigned to a firewall security group based on the system’s function. Security groups restrict access to only the ports and protocols required for a system’s specific function to mitigate risk.
## Host-based firewalls restrict customer applications from establishing local host connections over the loopback network interface to further isolate customer applications. Host-based firewalls also provide the ability to further limit inbound and outbound connections as needed.
# *Infrastructure*
## Heroku’s infrastructure provides DDoS mitigation techniques, firewalls to prevent IP, MAC, and ARP spoofing on the network and between virtual hosts, and port scanning, which is prohibited.
## Each application on Heroku runs within its own isolated environment and cannot interact with other applications or areas of the system.
# *Data Security*
## The Processor has been subjected to security application and penetration tests and has also been tested against known vulnerabilities, using automated tool. The positive outcome of the penetration tests conducted on our system further reiterates our good security practices. Penetrations tests are completed from time to time by the Processor. 
## The Processor has strong access control policies in place to all services that it utilizes. Access to any part of its System is given to its staff only if it is a necessity. All access to either its System or third-party systems is protected through strong passwords and two factor authentication. 
## The Processor has advanced error reporting and logging systems running in the background. Whenever any diagnostic test fails or a system bug is detected, emails are sent to the development team and these issues are prioritized. For all incidents, the Processor follows a incident response policy. 
## Full-service level agreements are documented as part of the Agreement. This lays out all the particulars of support requirements from the Processor, together with the client's obligations to receive different levels of support for different urgencies. The procedures and protocol is provided in the Agreement.
# *Amendments*
The Processor is permitted to implement other technical and organisational security measures equivalent to the measures prescribed in this _Annex 5  to the DPA_.

Regarding the communications to Couriers, no communications should be sent, as discussed in the previous Legal Ticket.

About communications to Fleets in the documents above, there are some comms we cannot send:

* *Communication Issues due to Language* - we cannot make language requirements to Couriers.
* *Fake GPS* - GPS usage is not mandatory and this has been a focal point in reclassification cases, with Courts stating in their Sentences “_The courier is free to choose the route he or she wishes to take for each delivery, as well as the time each delivery may take, choosing the GPS system he or she wishes to use for the route, or not using it at all, or even switching it off_.”
* *Courier entering wrong amounts* - I don’t think this is applicable to Portugal, as all payments are in-app, correct?
* *Using Wrong Vehicle Type* - Is this applicable to Portugal? Anyway, the Couriers are not obliged to use any type of vehicle or to disclose that information. The only obligations regarding vehicles are the ones in item 3 of our T&C.
* *Delivering without Thermal Bag* - This has also been a focal point in reclassification cases, with Courts stating in their Sentences “_In addition, Bolt does not require the use of a “thermal backpack” (it does not even require the use of a “Bolt” thermal backpack, but only a thermal backpack) for all orders. In accordance with point 5.2 of the terms and conditions governing the relationship with Fleets, the use of a “thermal bag” - which may or may not be a backpack - is only required ‘if the order contains food, [...] in order to ensure that the Goods are delivered in safe conditions, to ensure health and food safety_”.
* *Courier was Rude* - we cannot make behaviour requirements to Couriers.
* *Needs Re-training* - Bolt does not provide training, and even if framed under guidelines, its not advisable to send suspension/blocking communications with this basis, unless there is a specific identified breach of the T&C.
* *Courier Dressed Inappropriately* - we cannot make any requirements about Couriers attire.
* *Courier hasn't cleared their debt* - I don’t think this is applicable to Portugal, as the Couriers are paid by the fleets.

Regarding the other comms, it’s advisable that DLA revises them before we proceed to sending.

Being honest, if this is a context of a a single Estonian city, I believe the risks of going forward with soft opt-in would be quite low for this limited scope - at least from ePD POV.

ePD soft opt-in would be unlawful mainly because those are leads who have not actually completed the registration, and no “service provision” occurred. While it's possible to argue that they’ve accepted our T&C and became our “customer”, I consider that it would be problematic position to defend with AKI. If we extrapolate this activity as global, with other EU regulators it would be even more problematic, as many local laws/guidelines require an explicit purchase or provision of service to occur.

Cross-targeting makes it a bit problematic too, although I agree it is possible to argue that we are promoting work opportunities which drivers are essentially interested in.

Hello [~accountid:712020:1a99e337-a650-4a85-a8ed-f0825a04e850] and [~accountid:5d50390ec6b9320d9ea58352], just to provide some clarity about local specifications about payments to Courts or to Legal Authorities (such as Enforcement Agents, etc.) in Portugal.

In Portugal, the payments made to Courts or to Legal Authorities are required by law (Portaria n.º 282/2013, of August 29) to be made by MB (ATM) reference or by DUC (which is a document issued within the legal software system used to process payments and match them with the correct case they report to).

These methods of payment are subject to automatic integration to the computer systems that supports the activity of the enforcement agents and Courts and are also linked to the specific process those payments report to.

These payments are not regular payments for purchases of services or goods, therefore they are not subject to any obligation from the recipient of the payment to provide an IBAN.

If we continue to not make the payments in the legally mandatory way, we may face penalties (including interest) and we can even have a judicial claim brought against us.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* On 1 May, User A (rider, [profile|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/133880223/overview]) messaged CS in-app ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/565519042]) claiming that someone was using their account in South Africa.
** User A flagged that the following third-party email was using their account: [grxw92qsjm@privaterelay.appleid.com|http://grxw92qsjm@privaterelay.appleid.com/]
** User A sent screenshots of the unauthorised trips (i.e., they seem to have access to the email address above). They do not match any trips taken on User A’s account (no trips for the past month). User A noted that no deductions had been made from any of their cards.
* Based on CS investigation, trips were taken by User B (rider, [profile|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/167841840/overview]). Order does indeed match up.
** Detail overlaps:
*** User A and User B have same first name but different last name (Stian Frogner and Stian Joacobsen).
*** User A based on Norway, User B based on South Africa.
*** User A and User B have different emails ([stianfrognerjacobsen@gmail.com|mailto:stianfrognerjacobsen@gmail.com] and [grxw92qsjm@privaterelay.appleid.com|http://grxw92qsjm@privaterelay.appleid.com/]).
*** User A and User B have different phone numbers (+4741245819 and +27646480889).
*** User A account created August 2022. User B account created April 2023.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Nothing to suggest that this is phishing, nor overlap of phrasing of email addresses.
* IMO, there is one of two explanations here:
** (a) *Phone number recycling*: User A used to own phone number ending in 0889. They created both accounts at the same time under different numbers and email addresses, and then phone number was reallocated to someone else (User B). User A is now getting notified about User B’s trips.
** (b) *Identity theft*: User B has stolen details of User A and used them to set up a Bolt account.
* In either case, very unlikely to be reportable (particularly as no financial detriment suffered).

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Ask User A:
** Do they own email address [grxw92qsjm@privaterelay.appleid.com|http://grxw92qsjm@privaterelay.appleid.com/]?
** Did they used to own phone number ending in 0889?
* Once I have better visibility on the nature of the incident, I will escalate to ODPO team.
* Depending on the explanation:
** (a) Two data breaches here - User A’s account and details of User B’s trips. User B’s account will need to be deleted.
** (b) One breach here - Details of User B’s trips. Up to Fraud whether to delete the account. In any case, we would get User A’s details removed.

*Query*

{code:sql}with provider_cases as (
  select
    p.created_date,
    p.id as provider_support_case,
    p.order_id,
    p.user_id as provider_id,
    ik2.issue_key as provider_issue_key,
    case when ik2.issue_key in ('added_wrong_items_to_the_order_provider','decline_order_provider','forgot_to_add_items_to_the_order_provider','incorrectly_compiled_order','order_items_are_out_of_stock_provider','part_of_the_order_was_left_behind_provider','unable_to_contact_customer_provider','want_the_customer_to_be_refunded_provider','wrong_order_taken_provider','courier_took_the_wrong_order_provider') then true else false end as asking_to_refund
  from ng_customer_support_spark.etl_data_api_support_case as p
  left join ng_customer_support_spark.fact_support_case_issue_keys as ik2 on ik2.support_case_id = p.id and ik2.issue_created_date >= DATE_ADD(CURRENT_DATE, -30)
    where
      p.user_persona = 'provider'
      and p.source != 'beehive_outgoing'
      and p.created_date >= DATE_ADD(CURRENT_DATE, -7)
)
select 
doo.provider_id, get_json_object(pp.name, '$.en-US') as name, doo.country,
count(distinct doo.id) as all_orders, 
count(distinct case when pc.asking_to_refund = true then doo.id else null end) as asking_to_refund,
count(distinct case when pc.asking_to_refund = true then doo.id else null end) / count(distinct doo.id) as asking_to_refund_rate,
count(distinct case when pc.asking_to_refund is not null then doo.id else null end) as orders_with_provider_ticket,
count(distinct case when pc.asking_to_refund is not null then doo.id else null end) / count(distinct doo.id) as provider_ticket_rate
    FROM ng_delivery_spark.delivery_order_order AS doo 
    left join provider_cases as pc 
      on pc.order_id = doo.id
    LEFT JOIN ng_delivery_spark.delivery_provider_provider AS pp --REMOVE LATER,TEMP JUST FOR ME
      ON pp.id=doo.provider_id
    where doo.created_date >= DATE_ADD(CURRENT_DATE, -7)
    and doo.state = 'delivered'
    group by 1,2,3
    having count(distinct case when pc.asking_to_refund = true then doo.id else null end) > 2 
    and count(distinct case when pc.asking_to_refund = true then doo.id else null end) / count(distinct doo.id) > 0.1
    order by 6 desc{code}

Hi [~accountid:712020:dc012e17-7e04-4ad8-8750-81fc7f7c6047] , following our discussion previously, I’ve aligned within my team on our position regarding the talks of reopening GDPR/raising the issues we see. Generally speaking, our position is aligned with EUTA’s - we do not want to reopen the discussion on GDPR, as it might bring even more complexity and require enormous resources for compliance. However, below are some gaps we are facing with the current GDPR setup, sharing with you for visibility:



* *_Unclear rules around automated decision-making (Article 22) create a lot of grey areas_*
** It's tough to know whether certain platform features, like automated pricing or fraud detection, count as “solely automated decisions” with a significant effect on users. We often overcompensate to stay safe, which slows down product development and makes it harder to launch features consistently across markets.
** The “legal or similarly significant effect” threshold is unclear and inconsistently applied - We often can’t tell whether a decision like temporary deactivation, pricing adjustments, or lower visibility in search results meets this threshold. Different regulators interpret it differently, which makes it hard to scale compliance across markets.
** *_RoPA is more of a checkbox exercise than something useful_*
*** Maintaining detailed records of all processing activities takes a lot of effort, especially in fast-moving environments. But the actual business or compliance value of those records is often minimal.
* *_Data minimisation and purpose limitation rules are too rigid for how tech companies work_*
** We collect data to provide services, but it's also useful for improving models or flagging harmful behaviour. The GDPR makes it really hard to reuse that data, even when it's in the user’s interest. The lack of clear rules around what's a "compatible purpose" creates internal blockers and complicates our governance processes.
* *_Joint controllership rules don’t reflect how modern partnerships work_*
** Whenever we work with third parties, there's confusion over who’s a controller and what needs to go into the contract. That leads to long negotiations and conservative agreements that don’t match the actual risk or reality.
* *_Strict purpose limitation makes it hard to iterate on products_*
** When we want to adapt a feature based on how users are interacting with it, it can trigger a full re-assessment of the original processing purpose. This slows down teams and creates friction in product development.
* *_Cross-border data transfers are still a huge blocker_*
** Even with new SCCs, we still have to do transfer impact assessments for most vendors. The rules are unclear and unevenly enforced, and this adds a lot of overhead without improving privacy outcomes. A more practical, risk-based approach would go a long way.

*Introduction*

This procedure defines how compliance and regulatory risks are assessed, prioritised, and acted upon at Bolt. It provides a unified workflow combining legal and policy validation, risk scoring, and structured approvals, ensuring consistent, risk-informed decisions on product change requests driven by regulatory needs.

*Workflow Overview*

# *A product request is raised in Jira*
## Business flags a (compliance-related) product gap (e.g. via #rides-compliance, #rides-safety)
## Legal, Public Policy, and the Risk and Compliance teams identify or are informed of 
### new laws or regulations; or 
### changes in existing laws or regulations that will come into effect; or
### shifting regulatory landscape.
## -> The product request flows into Jira.
# *Key info on the nature of the request is gathered via the prioritisation questions*
## Legal, Public Policy and Local Operations teams validate the regulatory basis of the request by completing a set of prioritisation questions to assess the urgency and legal exposure.
## {{Insert questions}}
## Each answer is scored using a predefined scoring logic and the total determines the initial *Prioritisation Level*:
### P1 = High urgency (8+ points)
### P2 = Medium urgency (6–7 points)
### P3 = Low urgency (≤5 points)
# *A risk assessment is conducted*
## Product and Central Ops teams assign a *Risk Score* based on: 
### Impact (regulatory, financial, reputational); and
### Likelihood (based on Bolt and competitor history and forecasts).
## {{Insert likelihood x impact = risk matrix table}}
## This yields a *Risk Score* (Low to Significant), which guides the next step.
# *The product request is evaluated and prioritised* 
## Using both the *Prioritisation Level* and *Risk Score*, the request is evaluated by Central Ops and Product and a decision is made on how to treat the request:
### Accept
### Mitigate
### Transfer
### Avoid
# *A decision is made whether the product request is added to the roadmap*
## Based on the *Risk Score*, relevant stakeholder(s) approve or reject the decision on how to treat the request:
### If the request is approved, the request is actioned and monitored through delivery.
### If the request is denied, the risk is documented, tracked, and monitored continuously. 
## Relevant teams are informed of the decision based on the risk treatment decision-making flow (*WIP*).

* Note that there's *no limitation of liability under the contract* (except for that indirect damages are carved out, unless in case of gross negligence/intent).
* Subcontractors will undertake back-to-back liability towards us/indemnify us, and proper company insurance should be in place (as for any other tender, ping: [@daniel.severin|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U03KA2KSULF]), but overall exposure remains high.

* The tender requires drivers to have a visible ID showing their name and the supplier's name (i.e. "Bolt") (Sw. _Föraren ska inneha en väl synlig legitimation där namn och Leverantörens företagsnamn framgår.)_ [@elisabeth.gunnarsson|https://taxify.slack.com/team/U07MTRKCYGZ] as only authorities issue valid IDs, this may not be practically enforceable, but the municipality hasn’t clarified its position. Further note that the tender includes high penalties (SEK 1,500–5,000 (EUR 140–460) per breach and the risk of *immediate termination* for serious/repeated breaches. Hi [~accountid:712020:238a1b89-0f1b-4797-9066-90af4142a510] , the questions we have for Bolt Boost fraud/suspicious cases related to *both* anomalies and fraud. We will set up rules in the fraud engine based on the patterns that we found and we will be flagging orders which are anomalies. For more details on the exact scenarios refer to [+the following document+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/6098878465/UK+Driver+Benefits+-+Driver+Abuse+update+20+03+25]. 
*Questions for legal team*

* Q1: Relates to the first condition you stated: “*_Conduct a thorough review_*_: Confirm that fraud has occurred, not just a suspicion._”. 
** What exactly do we mean by *review*? In the case of national living wage compensation abuse, we will be looking at anomalies in the driver journey (e.g. distance between logged and estimated pick up time, estimated and logged trip duration). We will not have a human reviewer of each flag. The flagging of those transactions would be done by the fraud engine. We will send the flag to billing. Billing will recalculate the NLW compensation based on fraud signals. No human review is included in the process.
** In majority of these cases we cannot say with absolute certainty that driver intended to commit fraud. It could be the case that driver forgot to end the trip and instead of logging 15 minutes as it was predicted for that distance, the driver ended the trip after 3 hours.  We can say that it’s suspicious that the trip lasted 12x times longer than it should have, flag the transaction and exclude it from the NLW compensation calculation. For more details on the exact scenarios refer to [+the following document+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/COMM/pages/6098878465/UK+Driver+Benefits+-+Driver+Abuse+update+20+03+25]. 
* Q2: When we send this flag of a suspicious trip to billing, should they _exclude_ this ride from the NLW compensation calculation, or should they include the ride but use estimated values (estimated pick up, estimated ride duration and distance)? 
** Excluding the flagged trip from NLW compensation calculation would be a much easier solution for our development teams. 
** If we need to use estimated values, this would mean more work for Billing Rides development team. 
* Q3: Once the correction from Q2 is done, should there be some email communication to the driver? Right now we do not send them an email with details of the total NLW compensation amount. Do we need to let the driver know of national living wage compensation correction (rides we did not take into account)?
** Note: We will not block or suspend drivers. All we need to do is control which transactions are included in the NLW top up compensation. If we identify a large anomaly, we want to be able to ignore those trips from the top up calculation. Drivers will still be paid for the ride fare.

*Part 1: Legal Team Review Checklist (incl. Privacy review)*

|Clause|Purpose / What to Check|
|Regulatory Role Disclaimer|Ensure Bolt is not deemed a regulated payment institution or handling customer funds.|
|Funds Ownership & Safeguarding|Confirm Ecommpay holds and safeguards funds under its own license; merchant not considered fund custodian.|
|Compliance with Law & Licenses|Ecommpay confirms it holds all required licenses and complies with applicable law.|
|Warranties & Representations|Robust warranties by Ecommpay regarding service delivery, compliance, and authority.|
|Indemnities (One-Way & Mutual)|Bolt’s indemnity obligations limited; Ecommpay indemnifies for regulatory and data breaches.|
|Limitation of Liability|Liability cap for both parties; avoid unlimited liability except for core breaches.|
|Data Protection (DPA)|Confirm DPA/DSA is in place with annexes;|
|PCI DSS / Payment Security|Ensure Ecommpay is PCI Level 1 certified and merchant is not exposed to PCI scope (if using hosted solutions).|
|Audit Rights|Limited, risk-based right to request audit summaries or compliance attestations.|
|Confidentiality|Clear data and confidentiality protection terms; survivability post-termination.|
|Change of Control & Termination for Cause|Right to terminate on key changes or breaches.|
|Dispute Resolution & Governing Law| |
|Consequences of Termination|Transition assistance, final settlements, data migration.|

 

h2. Part 2: Commercial / Payments Team Review Checklist

|Clause|Purpose / What to Check|

|Territory & Market Scope|Confirm the markets covered match your operational footprint.|
|Fees & Settlements|Clear schedule of fees, payout frequency, and deduction method|
|Reserve / Collateral Terms|Check when and how reserves may be applied; define limits and release triggers.|
|Chargebacks & Risk Tools|Review who bears responsibility for chargebacks and how disputes are handled.|
|SLAs / Performance Metrics|Uptime commitments, transaction success rates, incident response.|
|Termination for Convenience|Ensure you can exit without cause with notice (30–90 days).|
|Automatic Renewal Clauses|Watch for hidden or silent auto-renewal traps; require express renewal or notification period.|
|Variation of Fees|Fee increases should require notice (30+ days) and merchant right to terminate.|
|Technological intergation terms (if any), subcotracting| |
|Exclusivity / Non-Solicit Clauses|Ensure there is no exclusivity, and push back on unnecessary non-solicits.|

Hey [~accountid:632ac798b2e3c5ad0fa1dd3e] This kind of upsell likely counts as direct marketing under GDPR, even if it's shown in-app. That’s fine, but we need to make sure users understand they might see promotions like this based on what they do in the app (e.g. cancelling a ride). If the nudge is triggered by behaviour, it’s good to keep it generic (not too personalised), limit how often it shows, and ideally give users a way to stop seeing it.

Avoid showing it in moments of frustration (like right after applying a cancellation fee) in a way that feels pushy, as that could backfire with both users and regulators. As long as it’s not overly personalised, is shown sparingly, and there’s transparency in the privacy notice, this should be low risk.

Also, a quick question before we go further: what channels are you planning to use for these upsell messages - just in-app, or also email/push?

Here’s some quick guidance depending on the answer:

* *In-app is* low risk if it’s shown sparingly, isn’t too personalised, and there’s clear language. Make sure it’s easy to dismiss and doesn’t interrupt core actions like cancelling or booking a ride.
* *Email/push* will likely count as direct marketing and we won’t be able to send comms to unsubscribed users.

I checked with [~accountid:626fb920f42962006fde4c04] and we concluded:

* According to the *EU Blue Guide*, the planned activity qualifies as *maintenance*, not a substantial modification triggering “new placement on the market.”
* As such, there is *no requirement* to re-label the batteries or re-register under *Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)*.
* Renting or operating scooters using these batteries does *not restart the compliance clock*, as the batteries were already placed on the EU market at first import.

Hence, TWS and Techsum shall remain as the manufacturers of the refurbished batteries. Also, to not mess up the internal data and to keep the battery history, the ID of the battery shall remain unchanged after refurbishing.

Pursuant to the clause 13.3 of the General Terms and Conditions for Couriers, Bolt is liable for damage or lost profits that the Courier may suffer only in cases where Bolt *intentionally or through gross negligence* violates these General Terms and Conditions.According to the clause 13.4. of the General Terms and Conditions for Couriers, the Courier shall indemnify and hold Bolt harmless from and against any and all claims, suits, actions or administrative proceedings, demands, losses, damages and expenses of any kind, including attorneys' fees and costs, arising out of or in connection with the delivery services provided by the Courier under these General Terms and Conditions. This provision imposes a broad indemnity obligation on the Courier for liabilities that are connected with their service performance.Based on the facts presented, there is no indication that Bolt has breached any of its contractual obligations—whether intentionally, negligently, or otherwise—under the agreement concluded with the Courier. Accordingly, there is *no legal basis to hold Bolt contractually liable* under the General Terms and Conditions.The circumstances suggest that the alleged damage suffered by the Courier have arisen due to the actions or omissions of the restaurant (the Partner), which may have acted carelessly. Under the Article 6.263 of the Civil Code of the Republic of Lithuania, a person who causes damage to another must fully compensate for that damage, whether the harm affects a person, property, or, where legally applicable, non-pecuniary interests. If the restaurant’s conduct can be qualified as tortious under the Civil Code, the Courier has the right to seek full compensation directly from the responsible party, in this case, the restaurant.Given the above and as I see this situation the following options can be considered:

# Compensate the Courier for the damages suffered as a goodwill gesture, *without admitting our legal liability*, in order to maintain business relations.
# Respond to the Courier with a legal explanation of the situation, emphasizing the limitation of Bolt’s liability under Clause 13.3, the indemnity obligation under Clause 13.4, and advising the Courier to seek compensation directly from the restaurant based on tort liability principles under the Civil Code.
# Compensate the damage to the courier and then approach to the restaurant requiring to reimburse our costs in accordance with the clause 12.4. of the General Terms and Conditions for Partners which states that the Partner shall indemnify, defend and hold Bolt harmless from and against any and all claims, suits, actions or administrative proceedings, demands, losses, damages, costs, and expenses of whatsoever nature, including attorney’s fees and expenses in respect of or resulting from the performance of the services by the Partner under the General Terms.

Hello [~accountid:712020:46da73ea-bcbb-4b69-8e3e-ac27402d61bc]. Here is the analysis for transportation of animals in Portugal.

Article 8.º, 3 of TVDE Law states that “_The transport of pets cannot be refused, provided they are properly accompanied and accommodated, unless there is a valid reason, such as danger, health or hygiene issues_.”

This article raises questions, as it only concerns the transportation of pets, and does not stipulate obligation regarding assistance animals.

In Portugal, Decree-Law n.º 74/2007, of March 27, regarding assistance dogs, states several types of assistance dogs, as follows:

* Guide-Dog, which is a trained or in training dog to assist a visually impaired person
* Dog for a deaf person, which is a trained or in training dog to assist a  auditory impaired person
* Service Dog, which is a trained or in training dog to assist a person with a mental, organic or motor disability.

Article 2.º, a) of this legislation states that Assistance dogs, when accompanied by a person with a disability or a qualified trainer, may access places, transport and establishments open to the public, namely: Public transport, namely aircraft of national airlines, boats, trains, buses, trams, underground and taxis.

TVDE services have to be considered public transportation, given that it is a publicly available transport service with a lucrative purpose, as opposed to a privately owned vehicle used not for a economic purpose, but for private needs.

Article 3.º, 1 states that the right of access provided for in the previous article shall not entail any additional costs for persons with disabilities and shall prevail over any prohibitions or limitations that contradict the provisions of this decree-law.

And article 3.º, 2 states that the right of access cannot be exercised while the animal shows obvious signs of illness, aggression, poor hygiene, or any other abnormal characteristics that could cause reasonable concern for the safety and physical integrity of people or animals, or if it behaves in a way that disrupts the normal functioning of the place in question.

Article 5º states that service dogs are properly certified by the competent authority, with article 6º stating the following:

# _The assistance dog must wear, in a clearly visible manner, the badge referred to in paragraph 3 of the previous article, which shall have official status and identify the dog as such._
# _The accredited establishment responsible for training assistance dogs shall issue an identification card for both the foster families and the assistance dogs in training._
# _Without prejudice to the previous paragraph, the user of the assistance dog must be able to prove, whenever necessary, the following:_
_a) Identification of the animal as an assistance dog, as defined in the previous article, without prejudice to other applicable legislation, namely that concerning the protection of companion animals;_
_b) Compliance with legally required health regulations;_
_c) Compliance with the obligations related to liability insurance as required under paragraph 2 of the following article._”

However, *these legislation is only applicable to service dogs, and not for other service animals.*

+*In conclusion:*+

+*Regarding certified assistance dogs*+*:*

* *The assistance dog should be certified and the certification can be requested to ensure right of access.*
* *However, right of access to a certified assistance dog can be denied if the dog shows obvious signs of illness, aggression, poor hygiene, or any other abnormal characteristics that could cause reasonable concern for the safety and physical integrity or if it behaves in a way that disrupts the normal functioning of the place in question.*
* *The rider with an assistance dog cannot be forced to use a more expensive ride-hailing service, as the right of access must not entail any additional cost to the rider with a disability.*

+Other animals that are not certified assistance dogs, (for example, the rider with a cat claims that the cat is an assistance cat, or an emotional support animal) - these animals are not considered under PT Law to be assistance animals, therefore they are under TVDE Law stipulations for pets in article 8º mentioned above.+

Regarding these other animals, there is other applicable legislation besides article 8º of TVDE Law.

Decree Law 315/2003, de 17 de dezembro, article 10º/1 states that “*_Animals shall be transported in vehicles and containers appropriate to the species and number of animals being transported, in particular in terms of space, ventilation or oxygenation, temperature, safety and water supply, so as to safeguard their protection and the safety of persons and other animals._*”

+*So, in conclusion, regarding pets:*+

* *The transportation can be refused for danger, health or hygiene issues, or if the animal is not transported in an adequate container, or even if the vehicle is not suitable for transportation (for example: if the pet animal is to big for the car, the driver can refuse the transportation).*
* *The owner is responsible for any damages caused by the pet, as per article 493º of PT Civil Code.*

Hi [~accountid:63314e9e9b32cfef93265252] I am of the opinion that you as an employees of private company are generally *not required to register as a lobbyist*, unless their activities clearly fall within the legal definition of lobbying as outlined in Article 2(1) of the Act.

There are several legal arguments supporting the position that registration is not required.

*1. Lobbying must be structured and organised*

Article 2(1) defines lobbying as:

“Structured and organised promotion, advocacy, or representation of interests in relation to public decision-making…”

If a Public Policy Manager only occasionally interacts with public authorities, provides information, or participates in consultations without a structured strategy aimed at influencing legislation or regulation, this does not constitute ‘structured lobbying’.

*2. Numerous exceptions to the definition of lobbying (Article 4 of the Act)*

PPM activities may fall under legal exemptions, such as:

* Article 4(c): Participation in meetings or consultations upon invitation from public authorities
* Article 4(d): Participation in public events
* Article 4(e): Publishing public commentary in media outlets

If the PPM is involved in expert consultation at the invitation of authorities, this is not classified as lobbying under the Act.

*3. PPM acts as an internal employee, not a professional lobbyist*

Although Article 2(3)(b) extends the term “lobbyist” to include employees acting on behalf of their employer, this only applies if lobbying is their primary and structured activity.

If the PPM focuses on policy analysis, internal advice, or general stakeholder engagement, and not on direct advocacy to influence laws or regulations, the legal threshold for mandatory registration is not met.

*4. Intent matters: purpose of the communication is key*

If the communication with public officials is not aimed at changing or influencing a specific legislative or regulatory act, but rather focused on information sharing, highlighting challenges, or open dialogue, then the activity is unlikely to qualify as lobbying.

*WHEN REGISTRATION MAY BE REQUIRED:*

Registration could become mandatory if the PPM:

* Regularly and directly communicates with public officials with the aim of influencing legislation or regulation
* Acts on their own initiative, rather than upon invitation
* Follows a documented internal advocacy plan or strategy
* Carries out formal lobbying efforts on behalf of the company in a structured, compensated manner

However, in order to be 100% sure, I suggest seeking formal clarification from the Commission for the Prevention of Conflicts of Interest (Article 7(4) of the Act).

Here’s my take on the situation:

The way Driver app presents price bidding rides is nudging drivers towards rejecting Ride Booker and Ride Booker API rides, because driver’s can easily learn that they can take less orders but earn the same or even more money.

Ride Booker orders are presented as regular orders in driver app as popup to accept the order but it’s easy to reject from driver side or if auto acceptance is off, then just ignore and wait for price bidding orders.

*Possible solutions*

Since we have to also cover our Ride Booker API partners, then any type of addition to Ride Booker itself is as last option. If we leave API customers out of the picture then we potentially create a lot of churn. Implementing support on Ride Booker API level + then helping all our partners to implement price bidding on their platforms + potentially API partners don’t want to deal with price bidding in the first place, because API is supposed to be convience of Bolt platform integration not some market/auction place.

*Things we can do to benefit both Ride Booker app + API customers out of the box*:

# Make Ride Booker orders visually look as higher priority orders in driver app
## _Similar to scheduled orders etc._
# In addition to point 1. incentivise drivers to earn more Bolt Rewards Points on Ride Booker orders, example 1.25-2x.
# Incentivise with simpy higher price/surge multiplier

*Things that require* *_heavy_* *development:*

# Implement price bidding support in Ride Booker app
# Implement price bidding support in Ride Booker API
## Coordinate integration on customers side, which potentially for some customers might mean ditching our platform due to large effort required for integration. Potentially difficult to upsell the whole price bidding value to API customers.

*Concusion*

My recommendation is to start with making Ride Booker order’s prioritised higher and provide icentives on driver (app) side of the things as this would cover both Ride Booker app + API customers.

*query*

{code:sql}select 
--round(fraud_payment_count_ratio, 1) as fraud_payment_count_ratio, 
--round(fraud_payment_amount_ratio, 1) as fraud_payment_amount_ratio, 
--case when successful_payments_trusted_sum < 1 then '<1' else 'not <1' end as successful_payments_trusted_sum,
case when amount_of_fraud_payments >= 60 then '>=60' else '<60' end as amount_of_fraud_payments,
sum(potential_fraud_loss_eur) as pot, sum(user_price_eur) as user_price_eur,
round(sum(potential_fraud_loss_eur)/sum(user_price_eur), 2) as fraud_rate
from (
select etl.order_id, etl.potential_fraud_loss_eur, etl.user_price_eur, prof.amount_of_fraud_payments,
CAST(get_json_object(dor.input, '$.additional.user_payments.successful_payments_trusted_sum') AS double) AS successful_payments_trusted_sum, 
prof.*
from ng_delivery_spark.dim_order_delivery as dod  
left join ng_profiling_spark.profiling_fraud_delivery_profile_by_provider_inapp_check_history as prof
  on prof.key = dod.provider_id
  and prof.created_date = dod.order_created_date 
  and prof.created_date between date_add(current_date, -120) and date_add(current_date, -60)
left join ng_public_spark.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders as etl
  on etl.order_id = dod.order_id
  and etl.order_type = 'food_delivery'
  and etl.created_date between date_add(current_date, -120) and date_add(current_date, -60)
LEFT JOIN archive_analytical.delivery_order_request AS dor
	ON dor.id = etl.fraud_calculation_id
	AND dor.created_hour between date_add(current_date, -120) and date_add(current_date, -60)
where dod.order_created_date between date_add(current_date, -120) and date_add(current_date, -60)
and prof.key is not null 
and dod.order_state = 'delivered')

Hello [~accountid:5d50390ec6b9320d9ea58352], for more context regarding your suggestion, please note that we have no legal grounds to support our claim that we can only process payments through IBAN references or to not proceed with the payments at all.

If Bolt has verified and confirmed, to the Court or Enforcement Agent, the existence of a pending credit to an entity (partner or other), and that credit has been seized on judicial order, we are obligated to deliver that amount to the Court or Enforcement Agent in charge of the collection, regardless of the credit's origin or nature of the relationship between Bolt and the Partner.
The importance of the issue and economic impact is high since, as far as we know, no payments are being made, and the consequence of not complying with payment (in cases where Bolt has confirmed that the credit exists) is the reversion of the credit seizure against Bolt, in the full amount in question in each specific case, and the payment of fines, whose amount cannot be specified at the time, since it is determined by the Court in a case by case evaluation.

I understand that, in past situations, an Enforcement Agent provided an IBAN to receive payments. This is in breach of the procedure mandated by law and even though the Enforcement Agent may have facilitated the situation, this is something a Court would never do or has any means to receive the payment other than the methods provided, which is the situation in this other ticket [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/PFI-678164|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/PFI-678164|smart-link]

Hi [~accountid:5ece16662490cf0c09d78cae] Thank you for raising the ticket and what an interesting idea!

I'm well aware that you're already very familiar with this area, but I want to highlight that the main risk here is reclassification—specifically, the possibility that by requiring or incentivizing branding, drivers or fleets could be deemed employees, workers, or dependent contractors, rather than independent service providers.

In light of the recent Rohlík case, we need to be especially cautious, as vehicle branding was one of the key factors considered by the court in determining the nature of the working relationship.

That said, I believe we can still move forward, safely and strategically. My recommendation would be to:

* Limit this initiative strictly to fleets; avoid branding cars owned by individual drivers.
* Sign light B2B marketing agreements with the fleets. Payments should be clearly framed as marketing spend.
* The decision to brand should remain fully at the fleet’s discretion, to avoid any implication of control over drivers.
* Keep participation voluntary, with no penalties or consequences if a fleet chooses not to participate.

Please let me know if you have any further questions for me!

*Query eater*

{code:sql}WITH provider_stats AS (
    SELECT 
        date_trunc('week', dod.order_created_date) AS week,
        dod.provider_id, 
        COUNT(dod.order_id) AS count_orders,
        COUNT(DISTINCT dod.user_id) AS unique_eaters,
        COUNT(DISTINCT dod.user_id) / COUNT(dod.order_id) AS unique_rate
    FROM 
        ng_delivery_spark.dim_order_delivery AS dod
    WHERE 
        dod.order_created_date BETWEEN date_add(current_date, -150) AND date_add(current_date, -60)
        AND dod.payment_method_type IN ('processout', 'card')
        AND dod.order_state = 'delivered'
    GROUP BY 
        date_trunc('week', dod.order_created_date),
        dod.provider_id
)
SELECT 
    ROUND(unique_rate, 1) AS weekly_unique_eater_rate,
    ROUND(SUM(user_price_eur)) AS price,
    ROUND(SUM(potential_fraud_loss_eur)) AS pot,
    ROUND(SUM(reporting_fraud_loss_eur)) AS rep,
    ROUND(SUM(potential_fraud_loss_eur) / SUM(user_price_eur), 3) AS pot_to_price
FROM (
    SELECT
        dod.provider_id, 
        ps.unique_rate, 
        dod.provider_name,
        dod.user_id, 
        dod.order_id, 
        date_trunc('week', dod.order_created_date) AS week,
        etl.reporting_fraud_loss_eur, 
        etl.potential_fraud_loss_eur, 
        etl.user_price_eur
    FROM 
        ng_delivery_spark.dim_order_delivery AS dod
    LEFT JOIN 
        ng_public_spark.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS etl
        ON dod.order_id = etl.order_id
        AND etl.created_date BETWEEN date_add(current_date, -150) AND date_add(current_date, -60)
        AND etl.order_type = 'food_delivery'
    LEFT JOIN 
        provider_stats AS ps
        ON dod.provider_id = ps.provider_id
        AND ps.week = date_trunc('week', dod.order_created_date)
    WHERE 
        dod.order_created_date BETWEEN date_add(current_date, -150) AND date_add(current_date, -60)
        AND dod.order_state = 'delivered'
        AND dod.payment_method_type IN ('processout', 'card')
)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1{code}

h3. Update regarding E2 collections

After not seeing E2 decreasing after V122 update on D1.08 scooters, hardware powertrain performed further vehicle logs analysis on vehicles with E2. After lengthy research and validation, it was found that Oslo D1.08 scooters show multiple init_down and init_done cycles + intermittent E2 in two situations - after swapping the battery and after AI output reset is done (AI_POWER_OFF + AI_POWER_ON). If this situation arises, the CAN is crippled, but there was no clear reasoning as to why that happens and it seemed to be some unknown ECU-induced issue.

Most (if not all) D1.08 scooters in Oslo still have helmet locks attached and connected, but they are not being used due to the requirement being dropped. As a result, Backend re-configured the configuration to disable the helmet lock for all D1.08 scooters with *_helmet_lock_present/0_* set command. This means that the backend tells the IOT forcefully that it should not expect a helmet lock to be connected.

This situation turns into a problem when the *_helmet_lock_present/0_* is set, the helmet lock is still connected, and there is a battery swap/AI output reset, both of which re-power the helmet lock CAN module and initiate boot. Historically we have been aware of the helmet lock CAN module issue and it was mitigated on IOT FW side with a *_BMS output reset_* triggered by *_helmetlock_init_down_* which helped IOT detect such faulty helmet lock CAN module boots which crippled CANbus (vs. actually faulty helmet locks, resulting in the error rightfully tirggered after the sequence).

If the helmet locks will stay connected to the vehicles *and* Backend forcefully disables the helmet lock expectation from the IOT configuration and either:

* AI output reset is done…
* Battery swap is done…

… it is possible that the helmet lock CAN module goes into the known faulty boot-mode which cripples the CANbus of the scooter, manifesting in form of multiple init_down and init_done cycles + intermittent E2 in two situations, as described originally. As priorly, backend configured the IOT not to expect the helmet lock to be connected before, IOT will also not get the *_helmetlock_init_down_* condition to trigger the *_BMS output reset_*.



The scale and severity of this issue is validate by multiple factors:

# Helmet lock CAN issues were historically crippling scooters and causing negative feedback and increased collections.
# D2 scooters, which have the same hardware (excl. motors which are 500W), same firmware code (ECU, IOT, BMS), same AI module and *no helmet locks* are performing multiple times better than D1.08 scooters when it comes to collections (km between collections)
# [~accountid:5f896ba2e357dd006e937e5b]'s analysis that _SYSTEM_TOO_MANY_ERRORS_ collections and count of rides were not correlated (when looking at hourly breakdown), which would dictate that ECU errors are not appearing in a regular manner for all vehicles and HW is not failing in such mode when being used during orders.
# Certain days (public holidays and weekends), when [~accountid:712020:4b03e27a-3746-4bbe-b026-a11ab5e65aaf] did not manually send the AI output reset command to IOTs which presented AI communication issues, there were significantly fewer _SYSTEM_TOO_MANY_ERRORS_ collections triggered as opposed to working days when a reset was usually done ever morning/evening.

Current auto-acceptance logic still applies (new version planned for Q3):

* Driver may ask why didn’t they get the order if they had auto-acceptance enabled:
** If only one driver out of all the dispatched ones has auto-acceptance, the system will give the ride to this driver within 3 seconds unless another driver accepts it manually before that.
** If there are 2+ drivers with auto-acceptance to whom the order is dispatched, the system automatically picks one to give it to, but again, if someone else manually accepts before 3 seconds, it goes to that driver instead.
*** *The easiest explanation to provide to the driver is that if there are 2 or more drivers with auto-acceptance, it's a random system pick.*

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

Olá, pessoal. Boa tarde.

As mentioned before, we are currently not able to process any EUR payout in a different method besides IBAN/BIC payment. This is not some preference by our side but also a limitation as we do not operate under any Portuguese bank account and also, a law violation. 

According to Regulation (EU) No 260/2012 (SEPA Regulation), specifically Article 9-2, entities that accept credit transfers or direct debits in euros are legally prohibited from discriminating based on the country in which a customer’s payment account is held, as long as the account is reachable under the SEPA scheme. *This means that an entity must not refuse a payment or mandate a local account just because a customer's IBAN is from another EU or EEA country*, as long as the account is reachable under the SEPA scheme. This rule is designed to prevent IBAN discrimination and ensure equal treatment of all euro-denominated accounts within SEPA. *Refusing payments based on the origin of an IBAN—such as only accepting local IBANs or payment methods —is a violation of EU law.*

You can advise them that Bolt does not operate under Portuguese bank accounts, but under EU instead. In case of resistance on their side, please decline the rejection and get in touch with the Legal team for a proper action. 

I'm afraid we won't be possible to process the payout under another EUR scheme besides IBAN, as it would demand a high engineering, expansion and project development action. 

In case of a new IBAN got provided by their end, please raise a new ticket and we will be able to process the payout accordingly.

Kind regards,

Hey all! Sharing the feedback I got from Legal --- 

*1. For Less Severe Cases (e.g. discriminatory language)*

* If CS currently messages the driver with a summary of the allegation and asks for their comment, then we are already providing sufficient notice and following due process.
* In these cases, riders rarely request non-contact, and legally, there’s no issue continuing this approach.

# *For Severe Cases (e.g. sexual or physical assault)*

* CS already limits messaging to: _“Your account has been suspended.”_
* This is sufficient under most legal regimes, especially if:
** The message is immediate and unambiguous,
** It indicates suspension is pending a serious investigation (even if that exact phrase isn't used).

*Police Request Creates a Legal Basis to Withhold Notification*
If law enforcement (even informally) asks that the driver not be contacted—for example, in connection with a criminal investigation—then we can legally defer all notice to the driver .
Additional advice:

* Do not notify the driver at all in this case, and follow the instructions given by the law enforcement authority.
* Internally, document the police request (even if it’s verbal).

* Disparage Bolt, or
* Cause harm to Bolt’s brand, reputation, or business.

Here’s how the relevant clauses support this:

* *Clause 8.2* allows for termination where a partner "disparages Bolt" or "causes harm to Bolt’s brand or business." This could reasonably include disrespectful or abusive conduct toward Bolt staff, particularly if it reflects poorly on the company or negatively affects its working environment or reputation.
* *Clause 8.3* further supports termination without prior notice in cases of repeated violations, which would strengthen our position if this is not an isolated incident.

However, before proceeding with the termination, could you please confirm:

* Whether we have sufficient evidence of the incident(s);
* Whether the behavior is serious enough to be interpreted as disparaging or harmful; and
* Whether the partner has been formally warned or temporarily suspended already.

{code:sql}select 
    round(foreign_card_rate, 1) as foreign_card_rate,
    round(sum(user_price_eur)) as price,
    round(sum(potential_fraud_loss_eur)) as pot,
    round(sum(reporting_fraud_loss_eur)) as rep,
    round(sum(potential_fraud_loss_eur) / sum(user_price_eur), 3) as pot_to_price
    from (
select
    dod.order_id, dod.order_created_date,
    dod.provider_id, 
    dod.last_courier_id,
    dod.provider_name, 
    dod.country_code,
    etl.reporting_fraud_loss_eur, etl.potential_fraud_loss_eur, etl.user_price_eur,
    count(dod.order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY dod.provider_id ORDER BY dod.order_created_ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7' DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) as count_orders_7d,
    count(case when etl.country_code <> etl.card_country then dod.order_id else null end) OVER (PARTITION BY dod.provider_id ORDER BY dod.order_created_ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7' DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) as count_foreign_cards_7d,
    (count(case when etl.country_code <> etl.card_country then dod.order_id else null end) OVER (PARTITION BY dod.provider_id ORDER BY dod.order_created_ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7' DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)) / (count(dod.order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY dod.provider_id ORDER BY dod.order_created_ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7' DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)) as foreign_card_rate
FROM ng_delivery_spark.dim_order_delivery as dod
left join ng_public_spark.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS etl
    on dod.order_id = etl.order_id
    and etl.created_date between dateadd(current_date, -150) and dateadd(current_date, -60) 
    and etl.order_type = 'food_delivery'
where dod.order_created_date between dateadd(current_date, -150) and dateadd(current_date, -60) 
and dod.order_state = 'delivered'
and dod.payment_method_type in ('processout', 'card')
    group by 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9, order_created_ts, etl.country_code, card_country
    )
    group by 1
    order by 1{code}

{code:sql}select 
    case when avg_age_7d < 100 then round(avg_age_7d, -1) else round(avg_age_7d, -2) end as avg_age_7d,
    round(sum(user_price_eur)) as price,
    round(sum(potential_fraud_loss_eur)) as pot,
    round(sum(reporting_fraud_loss_eur)) as rep,
    round(sum(potential_fraud_loss_eur) / sum(user_price_eur), 3) as pot_to_price
    from (
select
    dod.order_id, dod.order_created_date,
    dod.provider_id, 
    dod.last_courier_id,
    dod.provider_name, 
    dod.country_code,
    etl.reporting_fraud_loss_eur, etl.potential_fraud_loss_eur, etl.user_price_eur,
    avg(CAST(get_json_object(dor.input, '$.additional.user.created_age_in_days') AS int)) OVER (PARTITION BY dod.provider_id ORDER BY dod.order_created_ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7' DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) as avg_age_7d
FROM ng_delivery_spark.dim_order_delivery as dod
left join ng_public_spark.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS etl
    on dod.order_id = etl.order_id
    and etl.created_date between dateadd(current_date, -150) and dateadd(current_date, -60) 
    and etl.order_type = 'food_delivery'
 LEFT JOIN archive_analytical.delivery_order_request AS dor
    ON dor.id = etl.fraud_calculation_id
    AND dor.created_hour between dateadd(current_date, -151) and dateadd(current_date, -59) 
where dod.order_created_date between dateadd(current_date, -150) and dateadd(current_date, -60) 
and dod.order_state = 'delivered'
and dod.payment_method_type in ('processout', 'card')
    group by 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9, order_created_ts, CAST(get_json_object(dor.input, '$.additional.user.created_age_in_days') AS int)
    )
    group by 1
    order by 1{code}

They have sent a new request to provide the rider information and have provided the following legal basis:
We recognise your obligations under the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018), particularly concerning third-party data. However, the law contains explicit exemptions and provisions permitting disclosure of such data under circumstances which I am going to mention such as these.

# Schedule 2, Paragraph 5(3) of the Data Protection Act 2018

This paragraph exempts data controllers from the normal restrictions on disclosing personal data where the processing is:

“…necessary for the purpose of, or in connection with, legal proceedings (including prospective legal proceedings), the purpose of obtaining legal advice, or the purpose of establishing, exercising or defending legal rights.”

This applies directly to the present matter, where disclosure of the attacker’s identity is essential to enable our client to bring a civil claim for damages arising from the assault.

# UK GDPR Article 6(1)(f) – Legitimate Interests

Separately, a lawful basis for disclosure also exists under Article 6(1)(f), which permits processing that is:

“…necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party…”

In this case, our client’s legitimate interest in pursuing legal action against an individual who assaulted him clearly outweighs any privacy interest the assailant may claim.

Particularly where wrongdoing has occurred, courts recognise that privacy protections must give way to the interests of justice.

Disclosure in this case is both necessary and proportionate, satisfying data protection and common law tests:

In the event that voluntary disclosure is not made, we may apply for a Norwich Pharmacal Order, which compels third parties who are “involved or mixed up in wrongdoing” (even innocently) to disclose identifying information.

The foundational authority for this is Norwich Pharmacal Co v Customs and Excise Commissioners [1974] AC 133, which has been applied in cases involving disclosure of identities for tort claims, including assault.

** Once the order finishes, the Courier app sends a signal to the Activity Recognition SDK to switch off the sending the updates.

+*PRIVACY ANALYSIS*+

* *General*:
** *Countries*: UK
** *Deadline*: Estimated go-live is 14 May 2025
** *Data categories*: {color:#ff5630}Needs further clarity.{color}
*** Basic identification data, contact data, location data and data on ‘possible fraudulent behaviour’.
**** No SCD here. Arguably only criminal offence data when actually flagged as a crime (rather than inconsistency with T&Cs).
*** Fraud is detected using the following methods:
**** Ride Did Not Happen:
***** Average speed - Using GPS location to detect illogical time and distance calculation.
***** Short rides - Unrealistically short distances and durations for completing a ride.
***** Not reaching the final destination without a logged destination change by the rider.
***** Predicted and actual distances, durations and prices do not match actual ones by a large margin.
**** Driver Did Not Pick Up Rider:
***** Driver started and finished a trip without moving.
***** Arrival / start statuses done for away from a pick-up location.
*** Ultimately, unclear how we detect such fraudulent behaviour, and whether this is new or something we are doing already.
**** Based on the above, it seems we are looking at GPS location and trip details (including prices, predictions etc.).
** *Purpose*: To prevent and address fraudulent activities.
*** In terms of whether the data is proportionate, this appears to be the case. We just need to remind the business of this.
** *Legal basis*: Legitimate interest (recognised by Recital 47 UK GDPR). No need for LIA.
** *Transparency*:
*** Driver privacy notice needs to be updated. This will be covered in the updated notice.
*** In suspension comms, drivers are informed unrealistic timescales and given opportunity to appeal.
** *DPIA*: PPRA mentions that one is required. 
*** This is arguable either way - technically, this is large-scale processing of geolocation data in an invisible manner, which lends itself to a DPIA. There is not much we can do to ‘de-risk’ that side of things - instead, we can ensure human review / transparency as de-risking features.
*** If we decide to conduct a DPIA, we can update the fraud prevention DPIA that we already have.
** *A22*:
*** It appears that case managers implement temporary suspensions and send warning messages (also with appeals). This suggests that human review is implemented.
*** PPRA mentions ‘scoring’ - presumably this is in error.
** *Third parties*: None involved.
** *DSRRs*:
*** We can provide order data to the user. However, we would redact fraud triggers from DSAR responses on the usual way.
*** Users would not be able to object to this, as we have an overriding interest in preventing fraud.
* *ICO considerations*:
** Generally not applicable - ICO investigation only dealt with driver selfie verification and suspicious payouts.
** Key points are: (i) suspensions should be subject to human review; (ii) processes should be clearly documented; (iii) we are sufficiently transparent about the blocks to drivers; (iv) drivers are given an opportunity to appeal
* *Risk profile*: {color:#4c9aff}*Medium*{color}

||*Risk*||*Mitigation*||
|*Bias / Exclusion*
If fraud detection system does not work as it should, there is a risk of unfair discrimination here|Ensure the system is designed in such a way as minimises inaccuracies.
Ensure clear lines of accountability for decisions made by the system.|
|*Intrusiveness / proportionality*
We are tracking GPS data among other things, which may be regarded as large-scale surveillance / intrusive by drivers.|Ensure that we are not processing any excessive categories of data, and that this is clearly documented.|
|*Automated processing*
Account suspension _may_ be regarded as producing a ‘significant’ effect on drivers, and so if fully automated this would be caught under Article 22|Ensure that any suspensions are subject to human review.|
|*Transparency*
A lot of the processing here would be regarded as ‘invisible’ by drivers.|Ensure the driver privacy notice is updated ASAP.
Rely on comms sent to drivers re suspensions - these are a good idea.|

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
+*CONCLUSION*+

We can proceed with this feature (/)  provided that:

* Fraud detection systems are robust and minimise the risk of false positives / discrimination (in particular, ensure clear lines of accountability).
* We are not processing any excessive categories of data when detecting the fraudulent activity.
* We have clearly documented processes in place, particularly regarding how the fraud is detected (e.g., data categories / triggers), what the thresholds are, and how case managers should handle such cases.
* Any suspensions of driver accounts here are not automatic, but are instead subject to human review.
* The driver privacy notice is updated (this is with Privacy Team).
* DPIA is not strictly required, but worth considering (this is with Privacy Team).
{panel}

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** What is the full list of datapoints that we collect to detect this kind of fraudulent activity? Is it just GPS data and trip information (e.g., pickup, destination, predicted price, actual price, etc.)?
** Are we already detecting such fraudulent activity, and we are just changing our response process? Or are we implementing the detection process in the UK wholesale?
** Why does the PPRA mention ‘scoring’ - is this an error?
** To what extent is human review involved in the _initial_ suspension of the account?
** Are the threshold for what constitutes an ‘unrealistically short’ journey clearly documented?
* Subject to responses, advise the business according to the ‘conclusions’ above.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge.

Cheers,
Afiba

To create new pipelines, the next scripts should be executed:

{code:sql}-- insert into the table taxify_campaign_operations.pipelines FLAT - Model Run pipeline
FLAT_MODEL_RUN_PIPELINE_ID = INSERT INTO taxify_campaign_operations.pipelines (name)
VALUES(
    'FLAT Model Run'
);

-- insert into the table taxify_campaign_operations.pipelines LPCT - Model Run pipeline
LPCT_MODEL_RUN_PIPELINE_ID = INSERT INTO taxify_campaign_operations.pipelines (name)
VALUES (
    'LPCT Model Run'
);{code}

Both pipelines should contain the single DS_MODEL action with the default configuration.
Surprisingly, on the LIVE environment, we have more GACs with {{bonus_max_value_coefficient}} equals to {{1}}.

{code:sql}FLAT_DS_MODEL_PIPELINE_ACTION = INSERT INTO taxify_campaign_operations.pipeline_actions (pipeline_id, action_id, config_override, execution_order)
VALUES(
    $FLAT_MODEL_RUN_PIPELINE_ID,
    $DS_MODEL_ACTION_ID,
    '{"generation_type": "FLAT", "bonus_max_value_coefficient": 1, "look_id": 21267}',
    1
);

LPCT_DS_MODEL_PIPELINE_ACTION = INSERT INTO taxify_campaign_operations.pipeline_actions (pipeline_id, action_id, config_override, execution_order)
VALUES(
    $LPCT_MODEL_RUN_PIPELINE_ID,
    $DS_MODEL_ACTION_ID,
    '{"generation_type": "LPCT", "bonus_max_value_coefficient": 1, "look_id": 21267}',
    1
);{code}

For all GACs, where the {{bonus_max_value_coefficient}} doesn’t equal the default value, we need to overwrite the configuration, by inserting record into the {{taxify_campaign_operations.pipeline_configurations}} with the overwritten configuration:

{code:sql}INSERT INTO taxify_campaign_operations.pipeline_configurations (entity_id, entity_type, pipeline_action_id, config_override)
SELECT
  gac.id AS entity_id,
  'gac' AS entity_type,
  $FLAT_DS_MODEL_PIPELINE_ACTION AS pipeline_action_id,
  JSON_OBJECT(
    'generation_type', 'FLAT',
    'bonus_max_value_coefficient', gac.bonus_max_value_coefficient,
    'look_id', 21267 
  )
FROM taxify_campaign_operations.growth_automation_config AS gac
WHERE gac.bonus_max_value_coefficient <> 1 AND gac.default_generation_type = 'flat';

INSERT INTO taxify_campaign_operations.pipeline_configurations (entity_id, entity_type, pipeline_action_id, config_override)
SELECT
  gac.id AS entity_id,
  'gac' AS entity_type,
  $LPCT_DS_MODEL_PIPELINE_ACTION AS pipeline_action_id,
  JSON_OBJECT(
    'generation_type', 'LPCT',
    'bonus_max_value_coefficient', gac.bonus_max_value_coefficient,
    'look_id', 21267 
  )
FROM taxify_campaign_operations.growth_automation_config AS gac
WHERE gac.bonus_max_value_coefficient <> 1 AND gac.default_generation_type = 'lpct';{code}

After configuring everything, we can update the GAC ↔︎ Pipeline association:

{code:sql}UPDATE taxify_campaign_operations.growth_automation_config
SET pipeline_id = $FLAT_MODEL_RUN_PIPELINE_ID
WHERE pipeline_id IS NULL 
  AND default_generation_type = 'flat';

UPDATE taxify_campaign_operations.growth_automation_config
SET pipeline_id = $LPCT_MODEL_RUN_PIPELINE_ID
WHERE pipeline_id IS NULL 
  AND default_generation_type = 'lpct';{code}
